translations.text: Om. May Mitra be propitious to us, and Varuṇa propitious; may Aryaman be propitious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be propitious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be propitious to us. Homage to Brahman. Homage to you, O Vāyu. You indeed are the perceptible Brahman. You alone I shall declare to be the perceptible Brahman. (You) I shall declare to be the right; (you) I shall declare to be the true. May that protect me; may that protect the teacher. May it protect me; may it protect the teacher. Om. Peace, peace, peace.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad, after three verses (homage to the Self that is knowledge, from which the whole world is born, in which it dissolves and by which it is upheld; homage to the teachers who of old explained all the Vedāntas by word, sentence and proof; and that he composes this exposition of the essence of the Taittirīyaka by his teacher's grace, for those who like the meaning made plain): the obligatory rites, which wear away sin already incurred, and the optional rites, for those who want their fruits, were treated in the earlier part of the text. Now the knowledge of Brahman is begun, to remove the cause of taking up action. That cause is desire, for desire sets one moving; those whose desires are fulfilled, having no desire, abide in their own Self and cannot be moved to act. To desire the Self is to have every desire fulfilled, for the Self is Brahman, and the Upaniṣad will say that its knower attains the highest. So attaining the highest is abiding in one's own Self when ignorance has ceased (2.7, 2.8).

Śaṅkara, the objections: (1) liberation, abiding in one's own Self, comes without effort: one does not undertake optional and forbidden acts, the action that has begun to bear fruit is used up in experiencing it, and the obligatory rites are done so that no fault of omission arises. (2) Or, since the unsurpassed joy called heaven is caused by action, liberation comes from action alone.

Śaṅkara, the reply to (1): actions are many. The actions of many births, with opposed fruits, some begun to bear and some not, cannot all be used up in one birth, so another body will arise from what remains (Chāndogya 5.10.7). The obligatory rites do not destroy the action that has not begun to bear: a fault is taught for omitting them, so they serve to avert that coming pain; and even if they destroyed anything, it would be the impure only, not the pure, with which they do not conflict. Nor, without knowledge, can desire, the cause of action, cease: the desire of one who does not know the Self is for fruits that are not the Self, while in one's own Self, always attained, desire cannot arise. And the omission of an obligatory rite is an absence, from which no fault can arise; the not-doing is only the mark of a fault that comes from sins stored up earlier (so the present participle in ‘not doing what is enjoined’ is in place), otherwise being would arise from non-being, against all means of knowledge. So ‘abiding in the Self without effort’ does not hold.

Śaṅkara, the reply to (2): liberation is eternal, and nothing eternal is produced; what is produced is not eternal. Nor can rites joined with knowledge produce what is eternal: ‘eternal’ and ‘produced’ contradict each other. Nor is liberation like the absence that follows destruction, produced and yet lasting: liberation is a positive being, and that such an absence ‘is produced’ is a mere manner of speaking, since absence has no distinctions of its own and is only spoken of through the being it negates. Nor is liberation eternal because the agent of knowledge and rites is eternal and their stream unbroken like the Ganges: agency is itself pain, and when agency stops liberation would break off. Therefore liberation is abiding in one's own Self when ignorance, desire and action, the causes of taking up (a body), have ceased; the Self is itself Brahman, and ignorance ceases by knowing it. For that knowledge the Upaniṣad is begun. ‘Upaniṣad’ means the knowledge: it wears away womb, birth and old age for those devoted to it, or brings them to Brahman, or the highest good is seated in it; the book is called so because it serves that knowledge.

Śaṅkara: Mitra is the deity who presides over the activity of prāṇa and over the day; Varuṇa over the activity of apāna and the night; Aryaman over the eye and the sun; Indra over strength; Bṛhaspati over speech and understanding; Viṣṇu of the wide stride over the feet. When these deities of the body give well-being, knowledge is heard, held and used without hindrance. The seeker bows to Vāyu and calls him Brahman to quiet the obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman: Vāyu is Brahman because the fruits of all acts depend on him, so ‘homage to Brahman’ and ‘homage to you’ both address Vāyu, indirectly and directly. He is the perceptible Brahman because, beside the eye and the other senses, he is outside, near and unconcealed.

Śaṅkara: ṛta is what is firmly settled in the understanding, as scripture and duty have it; satya is that same thing carried out in speech and body. Both depend on Vāyu, so the sense is ‘you I shall call ṛta, you I shall call satya.’ ‘May that protect me,’ the seeker of knowledge, by joining me with knowledge; ‘the speaker’ is the teacher, protected by being given the power to teach. The repetition shows earnestness. ‘Peace’ is said thrice to quiet the obstacles to gaining knowledge that come from oneself, from other beings and from the gods.

translations.text: Om. We shall explain pronunciation: sound, accent, length, effort, evenness, continuity. Thus the chapter on pronunciation has been stated.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: the Upaniṣad is chiefly for the knowledge of its meaning; so that care in reciting the text is not given up on that account, the chapter on pronunciation is begun.

Śaṅkara: śīkṣā is śikṣā with a Vedic long vowel: that by which the uttering of sounds and the rest is learnt, or the sounds and the rest that are learnt. Sound is a and the others; accent is udātta and the others; length is short and the others; effort is a particular exertion; sāman is evenness, uttering the sounds at a middle pace; santāna is continuity, that is, saṃhitā. ‘Has been stated’ closes the chapter.

words.meaning: with the radiance of sacred knowledge

translations.text: May fame be ours together; may the radiance of sacred knowledge be ours together. Now, therefore, we shall explain the secret teaching of the conjunction (saṃhitā) under five heads: concerning the worlds, concerning the lights, concerning knowledge, concerning progeny, concerning the body. These they call the great conjunctions. Now concerning the worlds: the earth is the prior form, heaven the latter form, space the junction, air the joining. So much concerning the worlds. Now concerning the lights: fire is the prior form, the sun the latter form, the waters the junction, lightning the joining. So much concerning the lights. Now concerning knowledge: the teacher is the prior form, the pupil the latter form, knowledge the junction, teaching the joining. So much concerning knowledge. Now concerning progeny: the mother is the prior form, the father the latter form, offspring the junction, begetting the joining. So much concerning progeny. Now concerning the body: the lower jaw is the prior form, the upper jaw the latter form, speech the junction, the tongue the joining. So much concerning the body. These are the great conjunctions. He who thus meditates on these great conjunctions as explained is joined with offspring, with cattle, with the radiance of sacred knowledge, with food to eat and with the heavenly world.

notes: Śaṅkara: the prayer for fame and radiance is the pupil's wish, for the pupil has not yet gained his end; the teacher has. ‘Now’: after the rule of recitation just given. ‘Therefore’: because an understanding steeped in the text cannot at once be brought down to the knowledge of its meaning, a meditation that stays close to the text is explained first. The five heads are five supports, objects of knowledge. They are called great conjunctions because they concern great things, the worlds and the rest, and concern the saṃhitā.

Śaṅkara: the prior form is the prior letter: one is to look on the prior letter of the saṃhitā as the earth, and so on. The junction is the middle, where the prior and latter forms are joined; the joining is that by which they are joined. ‘Now’ in each place marks the order of the meditations.

Śaṅkara: ‘knows’ means ‘meditates’, as the context is knowledge and as 1.6 says ‘meditate’. Meditation (upāsana) is a continuous stream of like cognitions, unmixed with unlike ones, on a support that scripture names; the word is used in the world of one who continually attends on a teacher or a king, and such a one gains the fruit. So here he who meditates thus gains the fruits from offspring up to heaven.

The e-text reads upaniṣidaṃ, mahāsaṃhitāyā ity ācakṣate and athādhijautiṣam; they are set right here to upaniṣadaṃ and mahāsaṃhitā ity ācakṣate, as the bhāṣya quotes them, and to athādhijyautiṣam, as the text itself has adhijyautiṣam twice in this anuvāka.

translations.text: He who is the bull of the Vedas, of all forms, who arose from the Vedas, out of the immortal: may that Indra (the Lord, Om) strengthen me with intelligence. O god, may I be a bearer of the immortal (knowledge of Brahman). May my body be fit; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my ears. You are the sheath of Brahman, covered by (worldly) intelligence. Guard what I have heard. Bringing, spreading and without delay making my own clothes and cows, food and drink at all times: then bring me that prosperity, rich in wool, together with cattle. Svāhā. May students come to me. Svāhā. May students come to me from all sides. Svāhā. May students come forth to me. Svāhā. May the students be self-restrained. Svāhā. May the students be tranquil. Svāhā. May I be famous among people. Svāhā. May I be better than the wealthier. Svāhā. Into you, O gracious Lord, may I enter. Svāhā. May you, O gracious Lord, enter into me. Svāhā. In you, of a thousand branches, O gracious Lord, I cleanse (my sins). Svāhā. As waters go down a slope, as the months go into the year, so may students come to me, O Ordainer, from every side. Svāhā. You are a resting-place close by: shine upon me, come to me.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: for one who desires intelligence and one who desires prosperity, the means to them are taught, a recitation (japa) and an oblation (homa); ‘may he strengthen me with intelligence’ and ‘then bring me prosperity’ show it.

Śaṅkara: the bull of the Vedas is Om, being foremost; it is of all forms because it pervades all speech (Chāndogya 2.23.3). The Vedas are the immortal; ‘arose from them’ means that when Prajāpati performed austerity to draw the best essence from the worlds, the gods, the Vedas and the vyāhṛtis, Om appeared to him as that essence, for the eternal Om cannot literally be born. Indra is the supreme Lord, master of all desires. spṛṇotu: may he gladden or strengthen; strength of wisdom is what is asked. ‘Of the immortal’: of the knowledge of Brahman, the cause of immortality. vicarṣaṇam: able, fit (‘may it be’ is supplied). viśruvam: may I be a hearer. The sense of the whole: may my body and organs be fit for the knowledge of the Self; intelligence is asked for that alone.

Śaṅkara: ‘sheath of Brahman’, of the supreme Self, as of a sword, being the place where it is found: Om is the symbol of Brahman, and in it Brahman is perceived. ‘Covered by intelligence’: by worldly intelligence, that is, its truth is unknown to those of common understanding. ‘What has been heard’: the knowledge of the Self and the rest, gained by hearing; ‘guard’ it: let me gain it and not forget it. These mantras are for the recitation of one who desires intelligence.

Śaṅkara: the mantras that follow are for the oblation of one who desires prosperity. acīram is aciram, ‘quickly’, with a Vedic long vowel; or ‘for long’. gāvaḥ stands for gāḥ. ‘Then’: after intelligence has been brought about, for prosperity in one without intelligence only brings harm. ‘Woolly’: with goats, sheep and the like. It is Om that is addressed throughout. svāhā marks the end of a mantra used for an oblation.

Śaṅkara: yaśaḥ means ‘famous’. vasyasaḥ is vasīyasaḥ: may I excel the wealthier among men of my own kind. ‘That you’: you who are the sheath of Brahman; ‘may I enter’, and having entered be not other than you; ‘enter into me’: let the two of us be one. ‘Of a thousand branches’: of many divisions; in you I cleanse my sinful deeds. aharjara is the year: turning by days it wears out the worlds, or the days are worn away, contained, in it. prativeśa is a house close by where weariness is put off; so Om is the place where the sin and pain of those devoted to it are put off. ‘Shine upon me’: show yourself to me; ‘come to me’: make me of your own nature, as metal pierced by quicksilver.

Śaṅkara: the desire for prosperity is spoken of in a section on knowledge because wealth is for rites, and rites are for wearing away sin already incurred; when that is worn away knowledge shines forth. So the smṛti (Mahābhārata 12.197.8): knowledge arises in men when sinful action is worn away; as on the clear surface of a mirror, they see the Self in the self.

The e-text reads pramayantu and gives a line śāmāyantu brahmacāriṇaḥ svāhā before śamāyantu …; here it is pra mā yantu, and the doubled line is left out, as the bhāṣya lists the five (ā mā yantu, vi mā yantu, pra mā yantu, damāyantu, śamāyantu).

translations.text: Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ: these indeed are the three utterances (vyāhṛti). Of them the son of Mahācamasa made known this fourth, mahaḥ. That is Brahman; that is the Self; the other deities are its limbs. Bhūḥ is this world, bhuvaḥ the mid-region, suvaḥ yonder world, mahaḥ the sun; by the sun indeed all the worlds grow great. Bhūḥ is fire, bhuvaḥ air, suvaḥ the sun, mahaḥ the moon; by the moon indeed all the lights grow great. Bhūḥ is the Ṛk verses, bhuvaḥ the Sāman chants, suvaḥ the Yajus formulas, mahaḥ Brahman (Om); by Brahman indeed all the Vedas grow great. Bhūḥ is prāṇa, bhuvaḥ apāna, suvaḥ vyāna, mahaḥ food; by food indeed all the prāṇas grow great. These four are fourfold: four by four are the utterances. He who knows them knows Brahman; all the gods bring tribute to him.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: the meditation on the saṃhitā was taught, and after it the mantras for one who desires intelligence and prosperity, which serve knowledge indirectly. Next comes the inward meditation on Brahman as the vyāhṛtis, whose fruit is sovereignty.

Śaṅkara: ‘indeed’ recalls the three vyāhṛtis as well known. Māhācamasya is the son of Mahācamasa; ‘made known’, with u ha sma telling of what is past, means he knew, he saw it. He is named so that the seer is remembered: remembering the seer is part of the meditation. Mahaḥ is Brahman, for Brahman is great (mahat); it is the Self (ātman, from āp, ‘to pervade’), because the other vyāhṛtis, as worlds, gods, Vedas and prāṇas, are pervaded by mahaḥ as the sun, the moon, Brahman and food. ‘Deities’ stands also for the worlds and the rest: all are its limbs, and so it is said that by the sun and the others the worlds and the others grow great, as the limbs grow by the self.

Śaṅkara: each vyāhṛti is fourfold. Bhūḥ: this world, fire, the Ṛgveda, prāṇa. Bhuvaḥ: the mid-region, air, the Sāmans, apāna. Suvaḥ: yonder world, the sun, the Yajus formulas, vyāna. Mahaḥ: the sun, the moon, Brahman, food. ‘Brahman’ among the Vedas is Om, nothing else being possible where words are the subject. They are taught again as ‘four, fourfold’ so that they are meditated on in just that order.

Śaṅkara, on ‘he knows Brahman’: it may be asked why this is said, when Brahman is already known from ‘that is Brahman, that is the Self.’ There is no fault: its particulars are still to be told, that it is found within the heart, consists of mind, and the rest down to ‘rich in peace’ (1.6); meaning to tell them, the text speaks as though Brahman were not yet known. So this anuvāka makes one sentence with the next, and the two teach one meditation: ‘as bhūḥ he is established in fire’ (1.6) shows it, and no word here enjoins a separate meditation. All the gods, being his limbs, bring him tribute once sovereignty is attained.
The e-text reads tat brahma, loka mahīyante, jyotiṃṣi, prāṇa mahīyante and caturdha; they are set right here to tad brahma, lokā mahīyante, jyotīṃṣi, prāṇā mahīyante and caturdhā.

words.meaning: the two halves of the skull

translations.text: In this space that is within the heart is this Puruṣa, consisting of mind, immortal, golden. Between the two palates, that which hangs down like a nipple: (through it runs) the path of Indra, (going out) where the roots of the hair part, having split apart the two halves of the skull. As bhūḥ he is established in fire, as bhuvaḥ in air, as suvaḥ in the sun, as mahaḥ in Brahman. He attains sovereignty; he attains the lord of mind; he becomes lord of speech, lord of the eye, lord of the ear, lord of understanding. And beyond that he becomes this: Brahman whose body is space, whose nature is truth, whose delight is in the prāṇas, whose mind is bliss, rich in peace, immortal. Thus, O Prācīnayogya, meditate.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: the other deities were said to be limbs of Brahman, the vyāhṛti mahaḥ. The space of the heart is now named as the place for perceiving that Brahman directly and meditating on it, as the śālagrāma stone is for Viṣṇu: meditated on there, as consisting of mind and the rest, it is perceived as plainly as a fruit in the hand. The path to becoming the Self of all has also to be told.

Śaṅkara: ‘that’ (saḥ) goes with ‘this Puruṣa’. The heart is the lump of flesh shaped like a lotus, the seat of prāṇa, pierced by many channels, its stalk upward and its face down, as is seen when an animal is cut up; the space in it is like the space in a jar. Puruṣa: he lies in the city (the body), or the worlds are filled by him. ‘Consisting of mind’: manas is knowledge (from man, ‘to know’), and he is of it because he is perceived by it; or manas is the inner organ, and he is the one who identifies with it or is marked by it. ‘Golden’: made of light.

Śaṅkara: for the knower who has perceived him so in the space of the heart, the path to attaining the form of the Lord is told. The channel called suṣumnā, known in the yoga texts, goes up from the heart, between the two palates and through the piece of flesh that hangs like a nipple between them, to the crown of the head where the roots of the hair divide, and passes out splitting the bones of the skull. That is the indrayoni: the path of Indra, that is, of Brahman, the door to attaining one's own nature.

Śaṅkara: going out by it through the head, the knower is established in fire, which presides over this world and, as the vyāhṛti bhūḥ, is a limb of the great Brahman: he pervades this world as fire. Likewise in air and in the sun; and as mahaḥ in Brahman, the whole whose limbs they are. Abiding in them as their Self, become Brahman, he attains sovereignty: he is himself the king, the overlord of the gods who are limbs, and they bring him tribute. Brahman, being the Self of all, is the lord of all minds and thinks by all minds; that he attains, and he becomes lord of all speech, all eyes, all ears, all understandings: the organs of all beings are his.

Śaṅkara: ‘whose body is space’, or whose body is subtle like space. ‘Whose self is truth’: whose nature is the formed and the formless (satya), or what is unfailing. ‘Whose delight is in the prāṇas’: whose play is in them, or in whom the prāṇas come to rest. ‘Whose mind is bliss’: whose mind makes only for happiness. ‘Rich in peace’: it is peace and it is rich, or it is found rich through peace. These further qualities belong with ‘consisting of mind’ and the rest. The teacher's words ‘meditate, O Prācīnayogya’ show earnestness.

translations.text: Earth, the mid-region, heaven, the quarters, the intermediate quarters; fire, air, the sun, the moon, the stars; the waters, herbs, trees, space, the body (of Virāj): so much concerning beings. Now concerning the body: prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, udāna, samāna; the eye, the ear, mind, speech, touch; skin, flesh, sinew, bone, marrow. Having set this out, a seer said: ‘Fivefold indeed is all this; by the fivefold itself one fills out the fivefold.’

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: the same Brahman that was to be meditated on as the vyāhṛtis is now to be meditated on as the fivefold sets beginning with earth. By the number five there is likeness to the paṅkti metre, which has five feet; hence all is fivefold (pāṅkta). The sacrifice too is fivefold, as the śruti says (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa); so to conceive all, from the worlds to the body, as fivefold is to conceive it as a sacrifice, and by that sacrifice one attains Prajāpati, who is fivefold.

Śaṅkara: the first five are the fivefold set of worlds, the next that of deities, the third that of elements; ātman there is the body of Virāj, since the elements are the subject. ‘Concerning beings’ stands also for the two sets concerning the worlds and the deities. Then three sets concerning the body: of breaths, of senses, of bodily constituents. That much is all that is within; what is outside is fivefold too. The ‘seer’ is the Veda, or some seer who had this vision. By the fivefold within one fills out, strengthens, the fivefold outside, the number being the same: the two are found to be one. He who knows all this as fivefold becomes of the nature of Prajāpati.

translations.text: Om is Brahman. Om is all this. Om: this is compliance, as is well known; and saying ‘O, make them hear’, they make the call. With Om they sing the Sāman chants. With ‘Om śom’ they recite the praises. With Om the Adhvaryu utters the response. With Om the Brahmā priest gives leave. With Om one permits the Agnihotra. A brāhmaṇa about to recite says Om, (thinking) ‘may I obtain the Veda’; and he does obtain the Veda.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: the meditation on Brahman as the vyāhṛtis was taught, and then on the same as fivefold. Now the meditation on Om, which is part of every meditation, is enjoined. Om, though a mere sound, when meditated on as the higher or the lower Brahman becomes the means of attaining it, for it is the support of both, as an image is of Viṣṇu (Praśna 5.2).

Śaṅkara: one should hold in the mind that this sound Om is Brahman. Om is all this, because all that is sound is pervaded by Om (Chāndogya 2.23.3), and what is named depends on its name. What follows is in praise of Om, since it is to be meditated on. ‘Compliance’: when one says ‘I do’ or ‘I shall go’, another complies with ‘Om’; this is well known. With the call ‘O śrāvaya’ they have the answer made. The Brahmā ‘gives leave’, assents, with Om. When one says ‘I offer’, leave for the Agnihotra is given with Om. ‘About to recite’: about to study, he begins with Om, thinking ‘may I take in the Veda (brahman)’, and he does. Or: about to bring himself to Brahman, the supreme Self, he says Om, and by that Om he attains Brahman. Since acts begun with Om bear fruit, Om is to be meditated on as Brahman.

translations.text: The right, and study and teaching (are to be practised). Truth, and study and teaching. Austerity, and study and teaching. Restraint of the senses, and study and teaching. Quiet of mind, and study and teaching. The fires, and study and teaching. The Agnihotra, and study and teaching. Guests, and study and teaching. The dealings of men, and study and teaching. Offspring, and study and teaching. Begetting, and study and teaching. The birth of grandchildren, and study and teaching. ‘Truth (alone)’, says Satyavacas of the line of Rathītara. ‘Austerity (alone)’, says Taponitya, son of Puruśiṣṭa. ‘Study and teaching alone’, says Nāka, son of Mudgala; for that is austerity, that is austerity.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: since it was said that sovereignty is attained by knowledge alone, it might follow that the rites of śruti and smṛti are useless. So that this does not follow, they are set out here, to show that rites are a means to man's end.

Śaṅkara: ṛta was explained (1.1). svādhyāya is study; pravacana is teaching, or the daily recitation (brahmayajña). ‘Are to be practised’ is to be supplied. Truth is speaking the truth, or as explained before; austerity is the kṛcchra penance and the like; dama is the stilling of the outer organs, śama of the inner organ. The fires are to be set up, the Agnihotra offered, guests honoured. ‘What is human’ is worldly dealing, to be carried on as it comes. Offspring are to be begotten; prajana is begetting, approaching one's wife in season; prajāti is the birth of a grandson, that is, the son is to be settled in marriage.

Śaṅkara: study and teaching are named with each, so that one who does all these still takes pains over them: knowledge of the meaning depends on study, and the highest good on that knowledge; teaching keeps it from being forgotten and makes dharma grow. Satyavacas (‘whose speech is truth’, or it is his name), the teacher of the line of Rathītara, holds that truth alone is to be practised; Taponitya (‘constant in austerity’, or his name), son of Puruśiṣṭa, that austerity alone; Nāka, son of Mudgala, that study and teaching alone, for they are austerity. Truth, austerity, study and teaching, though already named, are taken up again to show regard for them.

translations.text: I am the mover of the tree (of worldly existence). My fame is like the ridge of a mountain. My pure source is on high (the supreme Brahman); I am the pure immortal (Self), as it is in the sun. (I am) radiant wealth. I am of good intelligence, immortal and undecaying. Such is Triśaṅku's utterance on attaining knowledge.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: this mantra is for recitation, and recitation is for the arising of knowledge, as the context shows; this section is for knowledge and no other purpose is seen. In one whose mind is made pure by recitation, knowledge can arise.

Śaṅkara: the tree is the tree of worldly existence, whose nature is to be cut down; ‘mover’: I move it as its inner ruler. My fame is lofty as a mountain ridge. ūrdhvapavitra: ‘on high’ is the cause, and the ‘purifier’ is the supreme Brahman, made known by knowledge; it is mine, the Self of all. vājini: in the one who has food (vāja), the sun; as the immortal, the pure truth of the Self, is known to be in the sun from many texts, so I am that pure truth of the Self. ‘Radiant wealth’: that same truth of the Self; or the knowledge of Brahman, radiant because it lights up the Self, wealth because it causes the joy of liberation (then ‘has been gained by me’ is supplied).

Śaṅkara: ‘of good intelligence’: whose intelligence is all-knowing, being skilled in the upholding, arising and withdrawal of the world. amṛtokṣitaḥ: immortal and undecaying (amṛtaḥ, akṣitaḥ); or sprinkled with nectar. vedānuvacana: veda is knowing, the knowledge of the oneness of the Self; the utterance after attaining it. Like Vāmadeva, the seer Triśaṅku, become Brahman, saw this mantra to declare that he had done what was to be done. Its recitation is for the arising of knowledge: it is read after the dharmas of 1.9, which shows that to one who is engaged in the obligatory rites of śruti and smṛti, without desire, and seeks to know the supreme Brahman, the visions of the seers about the Self and the rest appear.
The e-text reads sumedha; it is set right here to sumedhā, as the bhāṣya has it.

translations.text: Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: Speak the truth. Practise dharma. Do not be heedless of study. Having brought the teacher the wealth he welcomes, do not cut off the thread of offspring. One should not be heedless of truth. One should not be heedless of dharma. One should not be heedless of one's own welfare. One should not be heedless of (acts for) prosperity. One should not be heedless of study and teaching. One should not be heedless of the duties to gods and ancestors. Be one to whom the mother is a god. Be one to whom the father is a god. Be one to whom the teacher is a god. Be one to whom the guest is a god. The actions that are blameless are to be done, not others. The good deeds that are ours are to be followed by you, not others. Whatever brāhmaṇas are better than we, you should refresh them by offering a seat. One should give with faith; one should not give without faith. One should give according to one's wealth. One should give with modesty. One should give with fear. One should give with friendliness. Now if you should have a doubt about a rite or a doubt about conduct: the brāhmaṇas there who can judge, who are engaged (in these), not urged by others, not harsh, and desirous of dharma, as they would act in that, so should you act in that. Now as to those who are accused: the brāhmaṇas there who can judge, who are engaged, not urged by others, not harsh, and desirous of dharma, as they would act towards them, so should you act towards them. This is the command. This is the teaching. This is the secret of the Veda. This is the instruction. Thus it is to be practised; thus indeed is this to be practised.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the anuvāka: this teaching of duties is begun to show that before the knowledge of Brahman the rites of śruti and smṛti must be done as a rule. The instruction is for the refining of the man; in one refined, whose mind is pure, the knowledge of the Self arises with ease (Manu 12.104; ‘seek to know Brahman by austerity’, 3.2). ‘Instructs’: to go against an instruction is a fault. Rites are set out first, before the knowledge of Brahman alone is begun; and once that knowledge has risen the Upaniṣad shows that nothing of rites is left (2.7, 2.9). So rites serve the arising of knowledge by wearing away the sins stored up before (Īśa 11). The right and the rest were taught earlier (1.9) to keep them from being thought useless; here, to rule that they must be done, since they serve the arising of knowledge.

Śaṅkara: ‘having taught the Veda’, the teacher then makes the pupil grasp its meaning; so one who has learnt the Veda should not return from the teacher's house without inquiring into dharma. ‘Speak the truth’: say what is to be said as it is known by valid means. dharma is the general word for what is to be practised. Having given the teacher the wealth he wants as the fee for knowledge, and with his leave taken a fitting wife, do not break the line of offspring: even if no son is born, effort is to be made by the rites for a son; this is why offspring, begetting and propagation were named as three (1.9). ‘Not heedless of truth’: untruth is not to be spoken even through forgetfulness, as the word ‘heedless’ shows. Heedlessness of dharma is not practising it. kuśala is action for one's own protection; bhūtyai: from auspicious action for the sake of prosperity. Mother, father, teacher and guest are to be honoured like gods.

Śaṅkara: ‘blameless’ actions are those uncensured, marked as the conduct of the cultured; others, blameworthy, are not to be done even if the cultured do them. ‘Our good deeds’: those of the teachers that do not go against scripture are alone to be followed, for their unseen fruit; not the contrary, even if teachers do them. ‘Better than we’: marked out by being teachers and the like, and brāhmaṇas, not kṣatriyas or others; their weariness is to be removed by offering a seat and so on. Or (dividing āsane na): in their seat, when they are met in assembly, one should not even draw breath, but only take in the essence of what they say. śriyā: according to one's wealth; saṃvid: the act of a friend and the like.

Śaṅkara: the doubt is about a rite of śruti or smṛti, or about conduct, that is, custom. ‘There’: in that place or time; ‘engaged’ goes with the rite or the conduct. saṃmarśin: able to deliberate; āyukta: not set on by another; alūkṣa: not rough, not cruel of mind; dharmakāma: seeking the unseen, not smitten by desire. ‘Accused’: charged by someone with a fault that is in doubt. ādeśa is the injunction; upadeśa the teaching, of fathers to sons also; vedopaniṣad the secret of the Veda, its meaning; anuśāsana the word of the Lord, or the instruction of all who are authorities. The repetition at the end shows earnestness.

Śaṅkara, the inquiry into knowledge and rites, the question: does the highest good come from rites alone, from rites helped by knowledge, from knowledge and rites together, from knowledge helped by rites, or from knowledge alone? First view: from rites alone; for only he who knows the whole meaning of the Veda, the Upaniṣads' knowledge of the Self included, is entitled to rites (Manu 2.165), the whole Veda is held to be for rites, and if the highest good did not come from rites the Veda would be useless. Reply: liberation is eternal, and what rites effect is known to be non-eternal. That liberation comes without knowledge, by not doing optional and forbidden acts and so on, was answered (note on 1.1): the action left over brings another body, and obligatory rites do not destroy it. As for the entitlement: meditation is other than the knowledge got by hearing. One is entitled to rites by learning alone; meditation is enjoined as a different thing with liberation for its fruit, as ‘to be reflected on, to be meditated on’ are enjoined as separate efforts after ‘to be heard’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.5).

Śaṅkara, second and third views: then from rites helped by knowledge; as poison or curd, which of themselves bring death or fever, produce another effect when joined with a mantra or sugar, so rites with knowledge produce liberation. No: what is produced is non-eternal. Nor is a produced thing eternal because a text says so: a text makes known what is, it does not make what is not; not by a hundred texts is the eternal produced or the produced made imperishable. This also answers the view that knowledge and rites together produce liberation. Nor do the two remove what obstructs liberation: rites are seen to have other fruits, namely producing, refining, changing or reaching something, and liberation is the opposite of these.

Śaṅkara, on reaching: if it is said that liberation is reached, as the texts on going show (Muṇḍaka 1.2.11, Kaṭha 2.3.16), no: Brahman is all-pervading, being the cause of space and the rest, and is not other than those who go; all knowing selves are non-different from it. One goes to a place other than oneself; what is not other than a thing is not reached by it (2.6; Gītā 13.2). The texts on going and on lordly powers (Chāndogya 7.26.2, 8.2.1, 8.12.3) concern the effected Brahman; women and the rest are there, not in the cause (Chāndogya 6.2.1, 7.24.1; Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.14).

Śaṅkara, on combining: knowledge and rites cannot be joined, for they conflict. Knowledge has for its object the reality in which the distinctions of agent and the other factors are dissolved; rites are accomplished by those very factors. One thing cannot in truth be seen both as having these distinctions and as void of them; one view must be false, and it is fitting that duality, the object of natural ignorance, is the false one (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.14, 1.4.10; Kaṭha 2.1.10; Chāndogya 7.24.1; here 2.7), and oneness the true (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.20; Chāndogya 6.2.1, 7.25.2; Muṇḍaka 2.2.11). Without seeing the difference of recipient and the other factors no rite is possible, and in the sphere of knowledge the seeing of otherness is denied a thousand times.

Śaṅkara, on the injunctions: it is objected that rites are enjoined; if the knowledge of oneness wipes out the factors of action, as knowledge of the rope wipes out the snake, the texts enjoining rites lose their object, and scripture, being authoritative, cannot conflict with itself. Reply: scripture aims at teaching man's good. The texts on knowledge proceed to reveal knowledge, since man is to be freed from worldly existence and its cause, ignorance, removed by knowledge. The texts on rites do not teach that the factors of action exist; taking their existence as commonly accepted, they enjoin rites for wearing away sin incurred, for seekers of liberation, and as means to fruits for those who want fruits. In one obstructed by stored-up sin knowledge does not arise; when that is worn away knowledge arises, then ignorance ceases, then worldly existence ends for good. Again: he who sees what is not the Self desires what is not the Self; desiring, he acts; thence worldly existence, the taking of bodies to enjoy the fruits. For him who sees the oneness of the Self there is no object, so no desire; and abiding in one's own Self is liberation. For this reason too knowledge and rites conflict, and knowledge does not depend on rites for liberation. But the obligatory rites become causes of the arising of knowledge by removing the obstruction of sin stored up before; that is why they are set out in this section. So the texts enjoining rites are not contradicted, and it is established that the highest good comes from knowledge alone.

Śaṅkara, on the other stages of life: it is objected that then there are no other āśramas; knowledge arises through rites, rites are enjoined for the householder, so there is one āśrama only, and the texts on lifelong rites agree. Reply: rites are many. Not only the Agnihotra and the like are rites: celibate studentship, austerity, truthfulness, quiet of mind, restraint, non-injury and the like, well known in the other āśramas, are the best means to knowledge and are unmixed, and so are meditation and the fixing of the mind (3.2). Knowledge may arise even before the householder's stage from the rites of former births; that stage is taken up for the sake of rites, and when knowledge, which rites are to bring, is already there, taking it up is pointless. Sons and the rest are for the worlds; how should one act who has turned from this world, the world of the ancestors and the world of the gods, who sees the ever-attained Self and no use in rites? Even one who has become a householder, when knowledge arises and ripens and he is dispassionate, will cease from rites (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.5.2).

Śaṅkara, the last objections: the śruti takes more pains over rites, the Agnihotra and the like needing many means and much labour, while austerity and celibacy are shared by the householder and need little; so the other āśramas are not an equal option. Reply: the Agnihotra and celibacy practised in former births also help knowledge to arise; some are seen dispassionate from birth, others busy with rites, without dispassion, hostile to knowledge; for the dispassionate, the other āśramas are what is wanted. The pains taken over rites are explained by the countless fruits of rites (sons, heaven, the radiance of sacred knowledge) and men's many desires for them; and rites are the means, and it is over the means, not the end, that pains are taken. If it is said that, knowledge arising from rites by the removal of obstruction, the effort of hearing the Upaniṣads apart from rites is useless: no, there is no rule that knowledge arises only from the removal of obstruction and not from the Lord's grace, austerity, meditation and the like; non-injury and celibacy help knowledge, and hearing, reflection and meditation are its direct causes. So the other āśramas are established, all are entitled to knowledge, and the highest good comes from knowledge alone.

translations.text: May Mitra be propitious to us, and Varuṇa propitious; may Aryaman be propitious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be propitious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be propitious to us. Homage to Brahman. Homage to you, O Vāyu. You indeed are the perceptible Brahman. You alone I have declared to be the perceptible Brahman. (You) I have declared to be the right; (you) I have declared to be the true. That has protected me; that has protected the teacher. It has protected me; it has protected the teacher. Om.
